Beauhurst identifies ambitious businesses using eight triggers (outlined at 
the bottom of this page) that suggest a company has high-growth potential. 
More detail on Beauhurst’s tracking triggers is available via its website. 
equity investment 
To be included in the analysis, any investment must be:
•	
Some form of equity investment
•	
Secured by a non-listed UK company
•	
Issued between 1 January 2011 and 31 December 2020
announced and unannounced fundraisings 
An unannounced fundraising is an investment made into a private company 
that is completed without press coverage or a statement from the recipient 
company or funds that made the investment. These transactions are an 
integral part of the UK’s high-growth economy, accounting for around 70% 
of all equity transactions.

Future Insights: FoodTech 2021
We’re excited to be working with 
Beauhurst to produce this series 
of industry reports, examining UK 
companies that will shape the future 
of how we consume retail, media and 
food. In the first of three reports, we 
focus on how we eat, what we eat 
and the UK FoodTech companies 
transforming the industry. 
 
After a decade of rising social 
awareness, health initiatives and 
environmental activism, contemporary 
consumers want their food healthy, 
ethical and sustainably sourced. 
From the rise of meat alternatives 
and groceries-on-demand to AI-
powered AgriTech, the FoodTech 
sector’s future is increasingly guided 
by consumer attitudes towards 
conscious consumption, climate, and 
convenience. 
 
Not only are buyers more deliberate 
with their food purchases, but they 
are willing to pay more for the luxury 
of an on-demand lifestyle. This high-
growth ecosystem has led to a surge 
in FoodTech startups, fuelled by 
record levels of equity investment, 
grants awarded and successful 
crowdfunding campaigns.  This report 
equally highlights veganism and how 
a marginalised group has grown to 
over half a million people in the United 
Kingdom. The plant-based revolution 
has spawned over a hundred FoodTech 
companies in the UK since 2011, with 
London becoming a key European hub 
for vegan startups. 
 
With the world’s population predicted 
to hit nearly 10 billion by 2050, 
FoodTech innovation is becoming 
a moral necessity. Significant 
developments in agriculture and the 
global supply chain are needed to 
fight world hunger. As such, we have 
also chosen to highlight key AgriTech 
companies using data to increase 
yields, encourage sustainability and 
fight the effects of climate change. 
 
The rolling lockdowns of the ongoing 
COVID-19 pandemic supercharged 
the food delivery industry. Nimbler 
tech-powered startups are disrupting 
supermarkets and traditional retail. We 
take a look at some of the rising stars 
opening fulfilment hubs in London’s 
fiercely competitive grocery and meal-
kit delivery market. 
 
Huckletree is built on the motto that 
“No Mind is an Island.” We believe you 
can’t change the world alone, which 
is why we’re on a mission to help the 
most innovative companies, from 
startup right the way through to MNE, 
take leaps and do braver work together. 
We’re more committed than ever to 
creating the space and environment 
for teams to work, grow their ventures, 
collaborate together and pioneer 
whatever comes next. 
 
Our Futures Hub in Huckletree White 
City is home to some of the UK’s leading 
FoodTech companies. The campus, 
located within the iconic White City 
Place development, is part of a bold 
new chapter in the rich creative history 
of a neighbourhood that sits at the 
centre of West London – an area already 
brimming with high-growth FoodTech 
companies. It is a dedicated haven for 
startups and global brands paving our 
future way of life – how we sleep, think, 
move, and, of course, eat. 
 
We hope this report is both engaging 
and informative, and we’re very pleased 
that it’s landed in your hands.

Leo Medley,

Future Insights: FoodTech 2021
FoodTech is a growing sector where 
technology is being used to level 
up the food industry, making the 
production and consumption of 
food more efficient and sustainable.
The UK’s high-growth ecosystem 
has seen 863 innovative FoodTech 
companies launched since 2011. 
Of these, 650 are still active fast-
growing businesses, 67 have exited 
and the remaining 146 have ceased 
operations. FoodTech companies 
sit at the intersection of technology 
sectors, such as mobile apps, 
internet platforms or clean energy, 
and food-related sectors. These 
include food and drink processing, 
agriculture and farming, restaurants 
and cafes, other food outlets, 
catering, and waste management 
services.
Over the 10 years between 2011 
and 2020, these businesses have 
raised an enormous £2.6b in equity 
investment across 1,202 rounds and 
received £97.6m via 461 grants. The 
convergence of food and technology 
is an exciting area for investors and 
for the innovators seeking to disrupt 
the food industry at all stages of the 
value chain.

Future Insights: FoodTech 2021
Although the high-growth FoodTech 
ecosystem in the UK is still emerging, the 
industry has already seen the rise of some 
hugely successful companies. Household 
name food delivery services Just Eat and 
Deliveroo are just two of the industry’s giants; 
Just Eat exited via IPO in 2014, while Deliveroo 
did so in 2021.
 
The industry is also contributing to the wars 
against climate change and resource wastage, 
with many companies creating innovative 
ways to access food or inventing new and 
more sustainable production methods. 
Notable subscription-based businesses 
include Gousto, which achieved unicorn status 
in 2020 by offering a recipe box service, as 
well as D2C business Butternut Box that delivers 
cooked meals for dogs. In August, Butternut Box 
announced it had raised a new £40m round.
Map of Ag and Hummingbird Technology 
offer software and analytics technology 
for agriculture. Other companies want 
to revolutionise the food we eat, such as 
ENOUGH which produces mycoprotein as 
a sustainable alternative to meat, or Tropic 
Biosciences and which is developing new 
crops that are resistant to disease.

SPOTLIGHT: Karma Kitchen
Karma Kitchen		
London
Activity 
	
	
Commercial kitchen rental platform	
Incorporation date 
	
March 2017
Total funding raised	
£252m
Headcount (FYE 2020)	
5
Sisters Eccie and Gini Newton founded Karma Cans, a corporate catering 
company, in 2014. The pair went on to launch Karma Kitchen in 2017, drawing 
on their experience building two kitchens for Karma Cans. Customers can book 
Karma Kitchen’s commercial kitchens, production units and shared bench 
spaces online and use the flexible resource to grow and scale.
In July 2020, London-based Karma Kitchen raised £252m from Vengrove Real 
Estate Management to acquire properties to develop into kitchens. This deal is 
unusual compared to a traditional venture investment. Most of the money will 
go towards a newly created company that will invest in properties and lease 
them to Karma Kitchen. The remainder of the money will be used to grow the 
company’s existing operations. Karma Kitchen currently has sites in Hackney 
and in Wood Green but with £250m available for investment, it is well placed for 
further expansion.

There are innovative FoodTech 
companies popping up all over the 
UK to reshape the food industry 
with technology. Home to 234 
active high-growth FoodTech 
startups, London has the highest 
density of companies among all 
regions in the country — it is the 
natural geographical leader for this 
emerging industry.
Of the top 12 UK local authorities 
with the most FoodTech businesses, 
10 are located in the capital, with 
the leaders being Westminster, 
Islington and Camden. Some 
of the fastest-growing London 
Foodtech businesses include 
online supermarket Farmdrop 
for consumers to order produce 
directly from farmers, as well as 
FinTech startup Velocity, which 
uses Artificial Intelligence for 
recommendations and bookings for 
restaurants and other venues.
The local authority outside 
London with the most high-
growth FoodTech companies is 
Edinburgh, where 20 are currently 
headquartered. One such business 
is Qikserve, offering convenience in 
orders and payment for restaurant 
patrons through a self-service 
app, which has raised £11.8m of 
investment.

SPOTLIGHT: Hummingbird Technologies
Hummingbird 
Technologies	 	
London
Activity 
	
	
Imagery-based agricultural analytics	
Incorporation date 
	
June 2015
Total funding raised	
£14m
Headcount (FYE 2019)	
62
Hummingbird Technologies uses satellite imagery and machine learning to 
provide analytics to farmers and agri-businesses, allowing them to make better 
decisions based on data. The technology can help identify disease and weeds as 
well as assisting with yield predictions and sustainable farming practices.
Former investment banker and investor Will Wells started the business in 2015 
and has grown it to a headcount of over 60 serving more than 100 enterprise 
customers. The London-based company has secured £14m in equity investment 
via five rounds from investors including Newable Ventures, Horizons Ventures 
and the European Space Agency. It has also received five grants from Innovate 
UK and prevented the equivalent of more than 45k tonnes of carbon dioxide 
from entering the atmosphere.

Future Insights: FoodTech 2021
The annual number of equity 
investments into UK FoodTech 
companies has climbed steadily 
since 2011. The decade saw a total 
of 1,202 deals worth £2.6b. The 
top year for investment by value 
was 2019 which saw an enormous 
£687m worth of fundraising.
The company that secured the 
most equity investment between 
2011 and 2020 by far was Deliveroo, 
raising £1.1b in this period and 
then a further £132m in January 
2021. The unicorn food delivery 
company then underwent an IPO 
in March. The next five companies 
that raised the most between 2011 
and 2020—Karma Kitchen, Gousto, 
HungryPanda, Just Eat and Rekki—
secured a total of £602m between 
them.
For 526 of the deals made over the 
decade, it was the first time the 
company making the deal secured 
equity fundraising. With this 
number being almost half the total 
of the 1,202 deals, the FoodTech 
business ecosystem is clearly in 
its early stages. As more investors 
pay attention to the intersection of 
food and technology, the number 
of deals will likely continue to rise, 
particularly as investors follow their 
earlier investments.

SPOTLIGHT: Gousto
Gousto		
	
London
Activity 
	
	
Meal kit subscription service	
Incorporation date 
	
April 2012
Total funding raised	
£161m
Headcount (FYE 2020)	
702
Former investment banker Timo Boldt started Gousto in 2012 after experiencing 
the challenge of creating healthy meals at home while working long hours. 
Boldt started out printing recipe cards at home and delivered boxes of 
ingredients to homes across London.
The company now numbers among the UK’s unicorns. Its latest funding round 
in November 2020 valued the business at £780m. Customers can choose 
from more than 50 recipes a week to assemble a meal kit with just the right 
ingredients, helping to reduce cost and waste. Turnover hit £189m in the year 
ending Decmber 2020, up 130% on 2019 and driven by consumer demand 
during the pandemic. It is reported that the company is exploring an IPO that 
would provide liquidity for its investors which include Unilever Ventures, MMC 
Ventures, BGF and fitness guru Joe Wicks.

Future Insights: FoodTech 2021
The most popular way to raise equity 
investment among FoodTech companies over 
the last decade has been crowdfunding, with 
Seedrs and Crowdcube topping the ranking by 
number of deals. Crowdfunding platforms are 
an alternative means of financing, operating 
mostly online, and allow many investors to 
contribute funds. AgriTech company Hectare 
has secured seven funding rounds since 2015, 
with Seedrs either a participating or the sole 
investment source in every one.
Funds managed by Scottish Enterprise were 
involved in 39 fundraising rounds between 
2011 and 2020 worth £32.4m, supporting 
Scottish FoodTech businesses such as 
ENOUGH, Snappy Shopper, Qikserve, Insignia 
Technologies and Flavourly. Though yet to 
reach the scale of London, Scotland is also a 
key region for the rising FoodTech ecosystem.
The top four investors by value of the deals 
are all US-based funds. Each have invested in 
London-headquartered Deliveroo, which has 
raised £1.3b of equity funding and listed on 
the LSE in March 2021.

SPOTLIGHT: Cervest
Cervest	
	
London
Activity 
	
	
Climate analytics provider	
Incorporation date 
	
December 2015
Total funding raised	
£25.7m
Headcount (FYE 2019)	
19
This climate intelligence B Corporation was founded in 2015 by former 
agribusiness operator Iggy Bassi after he witnessed the devastation wrought on 
harvests by adverse weather events. Bassi worked with Imperial College London 
and the Alan Turing Institute to use machine learning to generate insights from 
climate data.
Cervest’s software now helps infrastructure operators, manufacturing 
companies, and governments to manage the asset and operational risk 
presented by flooding, fire, freezing and stormy conditions. It has raised 
£25.7m in equity investment, including a $30m round in May 2021 that included 
participation from Astanor Ventures, Untitled, and Time Ventures, which is the 
venture fund of Salesforce founder Marc Benioff.

11
Future Insights: FoodTech 2021
FoodTech companies operating in precision 
agriculture are the largest emerging sector 
group. Companies in this area are applying 
the latest advances in technology such as 
remote sensing and machine learning to 
tackle agricultural challenges. Hummingbird 
Technologies (page 6) is a company operating 
in this area, which uses Artificial Intelligence, 
which is the third ranked rising sector.
The second most populous group is 
services-on-demand, including the likes 
of Gousto (page 8) and Karma Kitchen 
(page 4). These companies are bringing an 
innovative approach to traditional consumer 
engagements with food and helping to reduce 
waste by allocating resources more efficiently. 
High-growth services-on-demand FoodTech 
companies, whether still active, exited or 
having since ceased operations, raised around 
£1.5b between 2011 and 2020.

Sustainability and FoodTech companies
The EAT-Lancet Commission on Food, Planet and Health highlights an 
agricultural, social and technological challenge facing the world; feeding 
a global population of 10b people by 2050 in a sustainable manner. All 
FoodTech companies are helping to tackle these challenges by finding 
more efficient methods of growing food, ensuring traceability of food, 
reducing food waste and finding more and better ways to recycle food.
Many FoodTech companies are mission-driven and are harnessing 
business as a force for good. A number of the companies captured in 
the data that underlies this report are Certified B Corporations. This 
is a private certification for for-profit companies which is granted 
only to “businesses that meet the highest standards of verified social 
and environmental performance, public transparency and legal 
accountability”. Climate analytics provider Cervest which is profiled on 
page 10 is a Certified B Corporation.
While the challenge of feeding 10b people within the next 30 years in a 
sustainable manner is a large one, it is positive that the UK has so many 
high-growth FoodTech companies that are contributing to a global effort 
to embrace more sustainable food practices.

12
Future Insights: FoodTech 2021
The vegan population in Britain 
quadrupled from 150,000 in 2014 to 
600,000 in 2019 according to research 
conducted by Ipsos Mori in 2019 for 
the Vegan Society. With concerns over 
health and diet, the environment, and 
animal welfare continuing to influence 
consumers, the FoodTech ecosystem 
has seen a rise in companies catering to 
a plant-based market.
Findings from Ipsos Global Advisor in 
2019 also revealed that half of people 
in Britain say they would eat a plant-
based substitute for meat, which is 
higher than the global average of 
four in 10. This suggests that this 
area is not just made up of those who 
are fully vegan, but consumers who 
want to simply reduce their intake of 
animal products.
Startups have a lot to offer this high-
potential market, including high-
protein sustainable meat alternatives, 
vegan snacks and drinks, plant-
based pet food, as well as meat and 
dairy-free ready meals and recipe 
kits on subscription. Investors are 
paying attention to these companies; 
£64m was raised by the UK’s vegan 
FoodTech companies in equity 
funding in 2020 via 51 deals. More 
than £90m has already been secured 
in 2021 so far, meaning this year is 
set to be a record high for the total 
amount of investment.
Spotlight industry: the rise of veganism
125
active high-growth vegan FoodTech companies
The UK’s vegan FoodTech ecosystem
London is certainly one of Europe’s hubs for fast-growing 
vegan FoodTech startups. Incorporated in 2016, allplants is 
a subscription service for vegan meals that has raised over 
£16m over five rounds of equity and loan fundraising. 
Meanwhile, producer of meat-alternative foods THIS has 
secured £20.5m in equity, most recently an £11m round in 
June 2021 for R&D. Investors included BGF Growth Capital, 
Backed VC and Five Season Ventures.
After attending the EIT Food Accelerator in 2019, Battersea-
based Better Nature has raised £2.4m across three rounds 
over 2020 and 2021. The startup uses fermented tempeh in 
its products to encourage meat-free eating.
Outside of London, Huel makes meal replacement powder 
from sustainable plant-based ingredients which offers all 
required nutrients. The Hertfordshire-located FoodTech 
startup has received £21m in equity investment and 
appeared on high-growth lists such as the Fast Track 100.
The international vegan FoodTech ecosystem
Vegan FoodTech companies are of course not only 
exploding in the UK, but around the world too. Oatly, a 
Swedish oat milk producer, is a major success story of the 
plant-based industry. The unicorn company raised $200m in 
2020 from investor Blackstone Group as well as billionaires 
including Oprah Winfrey, Jay-Z and former Starbucks CEO 
and Chairman Howard Schultz.
Danish firm Simple Feast provides vegan meal kits with a 
focus on sustainability. The B Corp secured funding of $33m 
in 2019 and recently entered the US market.

Future Insights: FoodTech 2021
A number of similar businesses are currently 
battling to win London’s express grocery 
delivery market, which has gained huge 
momentum since the pandemic and 
subsequent rise in consumer desire for rapid 
food delivery services. These companies offer 
a solution to frustration with deliveries from 
the UK’s major supermarkets, where slots 
need to be booked with advance notice, via 
the promise of rapid and convenient on-
demand order and delivery. Eight London-
based startups are profiled on this page, with 
most currently expanding their presence in 
the capital, while also hoping to extend to the 
rest of the country in the future. Elsewhere 
in the UK, DelivrMe from Birmingham and 
Cheshire-headquartered Beelivery are also 
quickly growing.
Competition is strong not only between 
each other, but from overseas competitors; 
German-based Gorillas and Turkish-founded 
Getir are already operating in London. US 
unicorn Gopuff is looking to accelerate 
expansion into the UK and the rest of Europe, 
while German company Flink has already 
arrived in the Netherlands and France and 
could have plans for the UK going forward.
Spotlight industry: 
on-demand grocery 
companies in London
Zapp and Weezy are not the only developing on-demand grocery delivery services. Grocemania, 
also in the seed-stage, was launched in 2016 and has secured £330k of equity investment 
through crowdfunding platform Seedrs. Meanwhile, Jiffy has raised a total of £2.6m; it launched 
during the pandemic and is planning fulfilment hubs across London. Devo was established in 
2016 and secured £70k in January 2020. Dija incorporated in November 2020 using a “dark store” 
model to meet pandemic delivery demand, then raised equity of £15m in December.  In August 
2021, Dija was acquired by US delivery unicorn Gopuff, supporting its European expansion plans.
Sustainability is a key focus for many on-demand delivery startups. Bother, offering AI-based 
software for users to order household essentials with the aim of reducing waste, has secured 
£4.9m of investment. Using zero emission electric bikes to deliver for supermarkets, e-cargobikes.com 
has taken three equity rounds worth £808k, and has previously worked with Sainsbury’s and Co-op.
Incorporation date 
	
November 2020
Total funding raised	
$100m (£73m)
Zapp has raised the most equity investment of London’s on-demand 
grocery companies at $100m (£73m); this took place across two 
rounds in November 2020 and March 2021 from VC firm Atomico 
among other investors. Stocking over 1,000 grocery items including 
drinks and snacks, Zapp operates a “dark store” model and promises 
24/7 ordering with delivery in 20 minutes or less.
International competitors
On-demand grocery delivery companies in London are facing fierce 
competition from the 2021 arrival of two major overseas firms. Both hold 
unicorn status, with Berlin-founded Gorillas reaching the valuation in 
just nine months, making it one of the fastest-ever unicorns in Europe. 
Getir launched in Istanbul in 2015 and operates in much of Turkey, 
and since raised an enormous volume of equity. With both promising 
delivery in just 10 minutes, the race to secure the London market is on.
Incorporation date 
	
September 2019
Total funding raised	
£15.7m
Weezy allows customers to choose from over 2,000 products —
including luxury items from independent brands — which it aims to 
deliver in 15 minutes. In January this year, it raised £14.7m to add 
50 more employees to its London-based team and to support its 
expansion to 40 fulfilment centres by the end of the year. It investors 
include DN Capital, Heartlane, and Left Lane Capital.
